module_title: DNS, Route 53 and Hybrid Name Resolution
review_basis: Original SAP Module 05 slide WebPs 7–10 inspected individually; narration follows depicted arrows, decisions and DNS caveats.
part_title: Hybrid Route 53 Resolver Inbound, Outbound and Resilience

scenes.title: Inbound Resolver: corporate DNS asks AWS
scenes.visual_overview: Corporate client queries its corporate forwarder, over VPN or Direct Connect, into a multi-AZ inbound Resolver endpoint.
visual_walkthrough: Follow client query to corporate conditional forwarder
Follow UDP/TCP 53 over private connectivity to the two endpoint IPs
Show private zone resolution inside associated VPC and response path
Explain SG, NACL, routes and DNS attributes
scenes.visual_example: An on-premises workstation resolves app.aws.example.com by sending queries through corporate DNS to AWS inbound endpoint IP addresses.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Inbound means DNS queries entering AWS, not remote queries directly to VPC base plus two.
scenes.narration: Read this picture from the corporate client on the left. It asks its corporate DNS server for app dot aws dot example dot com. That DNS server has a conditional forwarder for the private AWS suffix and sends the question over VPN or Direct Connect. The arrows reach Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint private IP addresses, deployed in two Availability Zones for resilience. Resolver then answers using the appropriate private hosted zone associated with that VPC. Follow the orange dashed response path back to corporate DNS and the client. The boxes underneath are the configuration checks. The corporate forwarder must point to inbound endpoint IPs, not the VPC base-plus-two address. The endpoint VPC must have private-zone visibility and the required DNS attributes. Network routes and security groups must permit UDP and TCP port fifty three, with response traffic allowed. The fact that name resolution works still does not prove the application's IP is reachable from on premises. For the exam, remember inbound refers to the direction the DNS query enters AWS.

scenes.title: Outbound Resolver: AWS asks corporate DNS
scenes.visual_overview: AWS workload sends DNS through VPC Resolver forwarding rule to outbound endpoint ENIs and corporate DNS over VPN or Direct Connect.
visual_walkthrough: Trace workload to VPC Resolver and associated suffix rule
Follow outbound endpoint ENIs in two AZs to target corporate DNS IPs
Review DNS SG, stateless NACL and route requirements
Explain PTR overrides and most-specific matching suffix
scenes.visual_example: An ECS task resolves db.corp.example.com using an associated forwarding rule that targets corporate DNS servers.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Outbound means query direction from AWS, and both forwarding rules and network routing are essential.
scenes.narration: This picture reverses the DNS direction shown in the inbound example. On the left, a workload in AWS asks the VPC Resolver for a corporate hostname. An associated forwarding rule matching corp dot example dot com selects the outbound Route 53 Resolver endpoint and its corporate DNS targets. Follow the cyan arrow through the outbound endpoint network interfaces in Availability Zones A and B, then through the private connection to corporate DNS. The purple response arrows take the result back to the workload. Below, the five cards explain the design dependencies. The rule needs the right domain suffix, target IP addresses and association with the client VPC. More-specific matching rules can be used when separate subdomains have different owners. The outbound endpoint security group must permit DNS to the target systems. Stateless ACLs and VPC routes must allow the request and return path. Reverse PTR queries can require explicit handling of corresponding DNS namespaces. The key distinction is that the outbound endpoint is responsible for DNS query egress; it is not an application traffic tunnel.

scenes.title: Hybrid DNS: give every suffix an owner
scenes.visual_overview: Top flow sends on-prem client queries to AWS private zone through inbound endpoint; lower flow sends AWS client queries to corporate DNS through outbound endpoint.
visual_walkthrough: Show AWS-owned aws.example.com resolved via inbound from on-premises
Show corporate-owned corp.example.com resolved via outbound from AWS
Explain why the two suffixes must not be blindly forwarded in both directions
Inspect DNS forwarding loops, delegation choices and UDP/TCP reachability
scenes.visual_example: AWS owns aws.example.com and on-premises owns corp.example.com; each side forwards only the namespace it does not own.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Define DNS authority and flow direction explicitly to avoid loops and outages.
scenes.narration: This visual combines the two hybrid directions but keeps their namespace ownership separate. In the upper cyan lane, an on-premises client asks for an AWS private name. Corporate DNS forwards the aws dot example dot com suffix to AWS through the inbound endpoint. The associated private hosted zone is authoritative for that namespace. In the lower orange lane, an AWS client asks for db dot corp dot example dot com. The VPC Resolver applies a forwarding rule and sends that request through an outbound endpoint to corporate authoritative DNS. The rightmost boxes make ownership explicit: one suffix belongs in AWS and the other remains on premises. Look at the caution cards along the bottom. Delegation is not the same as ordinary conditional forwarding. If each side forwards the same suffix to the other, a DNS loop can occur. Avoid sending every query through a broad root rule without a clear design. Finally verify UDP and TCP port fifty three in both directions, including routes and security controls. The goal is not simply to enable two endpoints, but to know which authority answers each namespace.

scenes.title: Resolver endpoints: security and resilience
scenes.visual_overview: Left panel shows inbound endpoint with ENIs in two AZs; right shows outbound endpoint with ENIs in two AZs and corporate target servers.
visual_walkthrough: Compare inbound destination 53 permits from corporate forwarders with outbound destination 53 to target DNS
Explain return traffic through stateless NACLs and private routes
scenes.visual_example: A single inbound endpoint IP or DNS target can create a failure domain even when the VPC is otherwise redundant.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Protect resolver ENIs and test both UDP and TCP 53 across the real network path.
scenes.narration: This slide puts inbound and outbound endpoints next to each other. On the left, corporate DNS forwarders send questions into AWS through an inbound Route 53 Resolver endpoint. On the right, AWS sends questions outward through an outbound endpoint to corporate DNS targets. Each diagram shows network interfaces in two Availability Zones. Those ENIs are the concrete network boundary where security group rules, subnet ACLs and routes become important. The bottom left security card says inbound endpoint security groups must permit DNS queries from approved corporate forwarders. The next card says outbound endpoint groups must permit DNS requests to the target corporate servers. The network ACL box reminds us that ACLs are stateless and must allow return traffic on the relevant ephemeral ports as well as DNS queries. The final resilience card asks for at least two endpoint IPs across AZs, multiple DNS targets, and capacity and failure monitoring. One last distinction on the footer: security group controls apply to Resolver endpoint ENIs, not directly to AmazonProvidedDNS. For troubleshooting, test both UDP and TCP port fifty three and check the actual forwarding chain.
